creator: Haruhiko Sameshima
results.description:
Diva, Paris was taken by Haruhiko Sameshima in 1992. It is a black and white photograph of an advertising poster in a bus shelter that Sameshima encountered while visiting Paris as part of a European trip at the end of 1992 and start of 1993. Sameshima used a Zeiss Super Ikonta camera to take this photograph, which used a two-and-a-quarter square inch negative. The camera, recently purchased by Sameshima, is essentially a 1950s tourist camera. The old technology, which was new to Sameshima, enabled him to take very different kinds of photographs to what his 4 x 5 inch Linhof camera would have. Because the Super Ikonta didn't require a tripod, it enabled Sameshima to document his European experiences just like any other tourist.
Luxurious signsDiva, Paris is a bus-shelter-advertising poster. The image explores relationships between specific places and global systems of representation and consumption. There is nothing stereotypical about this image. It is not a typical tourist site or image that signifies Paris. Yet the advertisement, which would not be out of place in Auckland, Sameshima's home city, is constructed around generic signs of glamour and luxury that originate in Europe, and cities like Paris, as the home of style and fashion. In this sense, Sameshima's photograph is a kind of investigation of signs, a seemingly straightforward image of the complex identities that result from the flow of signs - like photography and advertising - around the world.
SouvenirsDiva, Paris, along with Athene, another photograph in Te Papa's collection taken during the same trip to Europe, was exhibited in 1993 in an exhibition called Souvenirs at the Claybrook Gallery in Parnell, Auckland. As the title suggests, the show presented the best of Sameshima's 'tourist snapshots', and marked the beginning of his interest in tourism as a model for his own practice as a photographer.

Tūātapere history - Tūātapere Hump Ridge Track Official Opening, 2001:

Collection of images and records donated by Anne McCracken, a former Trustee, Associate Secretary Hump Track Trust, and Co-Convenor Official Organising Committee in 2001. These items are as listed below:
Images 1-3: Official Opening Programme and Ticket (number 500), 3pgs.
Image 4: Official Opening Poster for advertising the Track Opening event.
Image 5: Official Opening Invitation addressed to Anne & David McCracken.
Images 6-9: various items from the opening event - first is an Article from the news about the Track Opening and the School Choir practising the song written by Brian Ringrose; second is an actual photo of the Children singing this song at the opening; third is Brian Ringrose himself with his guitar, after singing his song on the Hump Ridge Track at the opening; fourth is a copy of the words of the song, "Let's Take A Walk", (c) Brian Ringrose.
Images 10-13: a selection of photos from the opening events - first is Mayor Frana Cardno speaking at the Official Opening Event; second is a photo of
someone else (unknown - can anyone identify this person please) speaking; third is Anne McCracken cutting the Official Opening of the Track Cake; and fourth is an actual photo of the beautiful Official Opening of the Track Cake.
Images 14-16: photos of various Official Opening day scenes - first is Anne McCracken with the Prime Minister and her husband Peter Davies; second is David McNay (Waiau Hotel Publican and Track Trustee) outside his hotel with the Prime Minister; third is the Prime Minister being taken for a ride on a horse and cart by Johnny O'Brien, in this photo outside the National Bank.
Images 17-19: lists of all entertainment & stalls for Opening event, 2pgs; email letter from Malcolm Garrett covering how the Opening event went.
Image 20: magazine article on Tūātapere Hump Ridge Track opening event.

THE OPENING EVENT:
An 'Official Organising Committee' was set up and this group met twice a month during 2001, to ensure that the Hump Ridge Track opening would be the event of the century for Tūātapere, even though that century had only just begun! Displays, Stalls, Events and more were planned over the two days of the Official Opening. The Prime Minister was to attend, who was at that time, the Right Honourable Helen Clark. Brian Ringrose, previously a member of the earlier popular 'Ray Columbus' band was to both write and perform a song about the Hump Ridge Track for and at the opening event. The school choir practised the song "Let's Take A Walk" and then performed this at the Hump Ridge Track Opening. Audio of this song is coming later.

As the year progressed and the Official Opening event drew closer, a draft programme was printed, then 500 of the final Official Programme brochures plus a large array of invitations to all and sundry from the town and region. One of the original Official Programme brochures (actually number 500!) & an invitation (to Anne McCracken and her late husband David) are shown. It was fabulous to also find that Anne had saved a raft of photos of the official opening event as well. Plus a few news articles and magazine features too. On the day itself, the weather did NOT play ball, it apparently rained, the wind was howling and everything and everyone was altogether soaked. But in true Tūātapere style, the locals soldiered on and the event was a success.


TRACK HISTORY:
The first idea of a Track to be created over the Hump Ridge in Western Murihiku Southland was brought to a Tūātapere Promotions meeting back in late 1986. After much groundwork on many legalities and formalities, the Tūātapere Hump Track Charitable Trust was formed after a public meeting in 1995. By 2000 the required Resource Consent had been granted by the Southland Council and finally the grand official opening of the track was held during 3rd - 4th of November, 2001. 

The Tūātapere Hump Ridge Track had been opened to walkers on the 1st November 2001, but the Official Opening event was scheduled to be held over the 3rd & 4th of November 2001. It is of note, that nearly 23 years later, on 25 October 2024, the Tūātapere Hump Ridge Track was Officially given 'GREAT WALK' status and again officially opened as the newest and 11th Great Walk of Aotearoa NZ, in an event held at the WTCC or Waiau Town & Country Club at Tūātapere. More can be seen on this on our CWA Facebook page, and further files will be put in these online collections soon.

Presently, from 25 Oct 2024 until 30 Nov 2024, a large display of history on the Hump Ridge Track is available to view at our Heritage Hub, which is situated at 48 Main Road, Tūātapere. We are open 10-4 Tues to Fri and the first Saturday of the month from 1-4pm. Contact us to visit at other times.


More information about the Tūātapere Hump Track Charitable Trust and the formation of the Tūātapere Hump Ridge Track will be added shortly. In the meantime, please share your memories of this important asset to our local community and stories over the years that you know of, and most of all, do let us know if you have any more photos you can share with us all please. You can do this by adding a comment about at the bottom of the image page, or making contact.

results.description: The value of understanding the diversity and impact of arthropod pests in grassland systems can be invaluable to plant biosecurity efforts by identifying new pests before they arrive in another country, whether through natural dispersal or via human-assisted pathways. The most commercially valuable crop in Aotearoa New Zealand, estimated to be worth $22B in 2025, is ryegrass (Lolium spp.) and clover (Trifolium spp.)-based pasture. A desktop-based investigation focused on a sentinel habitat approach to identifying potential macro-invertebrate risks to Aotearoa New Zealand pastures and associated crops. Predominately Australian literature sources were used to identify a range of native and exotic pest species associated with grasslands, specific grassland plants or crops. These invertebrate species were not known to be present in Aotearoa New Zealand. Overall, 129 macro-invertebrate species were identified as a potential risk. Of the species reviewed, c. 87 % (112/129) were Australian native and the remainder were exotic species. In terms of dispersal capability, c. 12% (15/129) were assessed as having a high risk of dispersing to Aotearoa New Zealand, with 71% (92/129) assessed as low risk. Dispersal risk was assessed on a range of factors including biology, flight capability and hitchhiking potential. In terms of impact on Aotearoa New Zealand pastures, c. 11% (14/129) were assessed as having high impact if they were to establish. These species belonged to Coleoptera (scarabs and weevils), Lepidoptera (moths) and Stylommatophora (snails). Clear limitations were found in relation to relying on the literature, as the sampling approaches did not capture temporal changes in pest presence, in particular missing migratory species. In addition, in some publications many insect species were simply grouped into taxa higher than species, in part due to a lack of expertise in taxonomic identification. Dispersal pathways including activities associated with trade and tourism, along with aerial dispersal via prevailing westerly air currents from Australia, mean that some of these species will arrive and establish. This ‘biosecurity over the horizon’ approach assists with risk analysis and decision priorities to target the most damaging invaders.

Jocelyn Buchanan, former Tauranga Jazz Society president, put together a visual history of the festival which showcased at Creative Tauranga from March 30 over the Easter period. This poster represented the 2000s.
 
The Noughties
2000
The Youth Band Competition remains an exciting part of the competition and is now held over two days with 25 bands competing for the trophies. The Festival places bands in bars in downtown Tauranga and later expands into Mount Maunganui.
2001
Think Easter, Think Jazz, Think Tauranga becomes the catch cry of the Festival with merchandise sold bearing the slogan. Merchandise sales always ran at a lost and ceased in later years.
2002
The city recognizes the Jazz Festival as a flagship event and funding is provided. The Youth Band Competition celebrates its 25th Anniversary with Northcote College winning the Best Big Band Trophy yet again.
200304
The Festival is recognized twice with the Bay of Plenty Tourism Award and also wins the Innovator Award. These achievements help renew Montana”s sponsorship.
200407
The breadth of jazz is expanded as gospel concerts are held at Holy Trinity Church on Good Friday. The growth of the Festival necessitates employing a paid administrator and Jo Bond (20062010) fills the position. In the age of the Internet www.jazz.org becomes the official website._x005F_x000D_
2008
As Montana ends its sponsorship of the Festival and volunteers are lacking, a smaller festival takes place. Streets are closed downtown to accommodate bands which appear on five stages. This shares the performers with all patrons and allows the bars and restaurants to provide food and beverages service. To control the “Downtown Carnival”, bars and restaurants require a special liquor license to take part. This action ensures they contribute to the event as well as taking great profits over Easter.
200911
The Festival has grown to such an extent that it can no longer be run by volunteers. Arne Hermann is appointed by the Tauranga Jazz Society as the Festival”s first professional Director. He in turn appoints an Artistic Director and project managers. Exciting new innovations include jazz on a steam train, river boat and the jazz village. Headline acts such as Blind Boys of Alabama, Dr John and Shorty Trombone bring performers to Tauranga that most kiwis would not expect to see live. Over 60,000 attend the Festival.

Collections of Images showing news items on the history of the town's first butchery, the now famous Tūātapere sausage, how the "Sausage Capital" title came about and Leo Henderson, who had claimed responsibility for the recipe.


IMAGES INFORMATION:

Photos and information on the story of how the famous Tūātapere - "Sausage Capital" of Aotearoa NZ came about, images donated by the descendants of Leo Henderson one of the LL Butchery partners, and by CWA Hub. NOTE: more information on the old butchery shop will be coming in a new entry soon, so watch this space. This CWA display advertising poster and its contents were created by the CWA Hub and unless otherwise specified, these are copyright or licensed to the creators of them, please see below.

2. Photo of the "Sausage Capital Sausage Shop" sign on the 'LL Butchery' Image by Zemlod, CC BY 2.5 - Created: 13 December 2005 (with thanks)

6. Photo of the prior Butchery Shop where the famous Tūātapere Sausages, were continued while owned by Tony Gillies from 2006. Taken in 2016 just before its demolition, by Larraine White and used here with permission.

7. New Tūātapere Sausage Capital sign, created and erected by the local Tūātapere & District Promotions Inc. group during 2022. This photo was gifted to us by them. It is licensed CC BY, so please attribute if re-using.

More photos of the Tūātapere Sausage "Big Thing" at its new home outside the Tui Base Camp Bar & Cafe, donated by "Jo and Darren's Supreme Adventure", look them up on Facebook, they are traveling, photographing, and blogging across the motu, around our country. These photos are licensed to the copyright holder, used here with their permission.

18. Winner Thomas Ramage of New World Alexandra, with his Beef Cheeseburger sausage, which earned him the title of New World’s Best Butcher-Made Sausage, here he is standing by the "Sausage Capital" sign.
This photo is a preservation copy from the Supermarket News site online.

19. Thanks to New World, a copy of the list of their contestants & flavours.

20. Current Logo of the Tūātapere Sausages, gifted from Tui Base Camp.

21. Information sign with the "Tūātapere Sausage" Big Thing at Tui Base Camp. But unfortunately, some of the information - which is very abridged and which was transferred from an earlier history situated on the Tūātapere Butchery building originally used to create the Sausage, is ambiguous at best (as it is taken out of context, no longer being situated on the shop).


TŪĀTAPERE SAUSAGE STORY:
Overview of how the Tūātapere - "Sausage Capital" title came about, in a copy of our information poster, photos and news articles over the years.

Poster of the history story of Tūātapere - "Sausage Capital": (quoted) 
"Tūātapere - Sausage Capital of NZ. The very first butcher shop, sadly now demolished  - [pictured] - The "Sausage Capital" Story: Back in 1988, in a 4ZA Radio Competition, the Butchery won the "Best Sausage in Southland", which led to the town's self-title, of Tūātapere, the "Sausage Capital of New Zealand" (Aotearoa). The title is not loved by all, but the label has remained, recently being revived by the New World Sausage Competition on 26 Feb 2026. Butcher "Leo". During his tenure, the famous recipe is created in 1971 - [pictured] - Sausage 'King' Leo Henderson's last day at work as owner of the shop - [pictured] - 1st Tūātapere Sausage Capital sign (replaced) - [pictured] - Tūātapere Butchery, "World Famous in NZ" - [pictured]." (end of quoted material)

In an interesting aside, the original Young & Aitken's butchery business in Tūātapere, was later owned by TJ Henderson for some decades, the grandfather of the now famous Tūātapere Butchery shop owner. After being sold to others, his grandson Leo Henderson was to purchase it back in 1971, with mate and ex-brother-in-law Len Kitto. They called their venture LL Butchery, as shown in photos here. Later, Len Kitto sold out and then Gordon Turnbull bought in with Leo. It has since been sold, and now closed.

It was the Leo and Len partnership, LL Butchery which first produced the now famous sausages. Some published news interviews have Leo claiming he was the one making the sausage recipe and trying it out on his family for years to perfect it, and in more than one interview with the butchery, the recipe is attributed to Leo. But in other interviews the famous sausages are credited to both Leo and Len together. Some of business partner Len Kitto's family members vehemently disagree, saying it was actually Len who had made the sausage recipe not Leo. We have put all versions of the sausage story here, to cover all bases. If anyone wishes to see any of these historical articles, please call in at our Hub, as they are in our Sausage Capital Files.

The sausages were a huge hit, the LL Butchery partnership were selling so many they had a special delivery truck to take them to all the butchers and stores that were selling them. It is fascinating to see all the news reports from those days and how popular these Tūātapere Sausages really were. And to understand the huge impact the sausages had on the LL Butchery.

After winning a local Southland Radio Station's "Best Sausage in Southland" (not a national competition as claimed elsewhere) in 1988 (and there are various dates reported for this - ranging from 1987 to 1989, however the most likely news sources seem to agree with 1988 (so does the family history of Leo Henderson & his family) and the loss of the town's staple industry, forestry, the village was struggling to survive, it is not surprising that they latched onto their new self-titled fame of "Tūātapere - Sausage Capital" of the country, with the erection of a new sign proclaiming this fact, which arrived not long after, in 1989. The butchery was bought and sold a few times, but the fame of the Tūātapere Sausage lived on, as can be seen recent news:

It was actually a later Butchery owner that entered a National Competition:
Article (quoted): "[Title] Tuatapere Sausages Ltd Wins Bronze, 3-12-2010, by Shirley Whyte in TUATAPERE. 
Tuatapere Sausages Ltd won a bronze medal for their pre-cooked beef sausage in the Great New Zealand Sausages Competition. Owner operators Vicky Harrison and Tony Gillies said they were stoked with their bronze medal as it was the only winning entry to come to Southland. “The win proves that our sausages are just as good as they 23 years ago... the Tuatapere sausage won a Southland radio competition for the best sausages with 87 percent of the listeners vote going their way. “To know that our sausage is still in the top three in New Zealand is pretty good,” Mr Gillies said. Tuatapere sausages make approximately 700 to 890 kilograms of sausages each week for the Southland and Otago markets and they can now been ordered on the internet and Face Book." (end)

Eventually the new and now "Great Walk" Tūātapere Hump Ridge Track opened and brought a new form of tourism to the town, but they still struggled to survive their losses for many years. The Tūātapere butchery closed, the recipe was transferred to another butchery, then that closed, and the Tūātapere Sausages ended up being taken to what was then the Highway 99 Cafe and Bar (now Tui Base Camp), so it thankfully survived. But, back to the story of how the town got its own giant Sausage statue (Big Thing)...

So in 2015, when ZM ran another Radio Competition to find the town most deserving of a large new monument, the listeners overwhelmingly voted for the town of "Tūātapere - Sausage Capital" to get their own giant sausage!! This was originally sitting outside the local Tūātapere Four Square (see photo) and was also to be shown in the town Christmas Parade, but ended up at Last Light Lodge. Unfortunately it was never meant to be permanent, so it became damaged over time, so had several refurbishments along the way.

The newly renovated Tūātapere Sausage recently moved to the centre of town, sadly minus its original fork, but now proudly sits at the newly named "Tui Base Camp" (Previously 'Highway 99') a Cafe with a Bar, Backpackers and Motels, where on any given day, many visitors and locals can be found enjoying food and beverage. They are also now owners of the "Tūātapere Sausage" name and sell their versions of these from the shop, with Debra Ellis, the Sausage 'Queen' carrying on Leo's & Len's (LL) tradition of making local Tūātapere Sausages, which are still a hit with tourists and locals alike. 

However, with the New World Sausage Capital event being held at the local Tūātapere Domain on 26 March 2026, and a new flavour, 'Cheeseburger Beef' Sausage being the highest voted and eventual winner, the town and its Tūātapere "Sausage Capital" title is again the centre of attention, which will not do us any harm at all. It is all rather amusing to many of the locals, who remain firmly divided on the whole Sausage Town identity. Some love it and others hate it. But despite that, it is certainly one claim to our fame!

The news of the day informs us, that at this event, New World officially crowned the country’s best butcher-made sausage, as part of a nationwide competition, which was judged by the people of the self-proclaimed ‘sausage capital of New Zealand’. New World Alexandra's Thomas Ramage took out the top honour with his Beef Cheeseburger sausage, which gave him the title of "New World’s Best Butcher-Made Sausage" after being voted the winner by the Southland town of Tūātapere, which is commented on as, "being known for taking its sausages very seriously." The competition came about, after a nationwide search across all the country's New World stores, where five finalist sausages were selected and brought down to Tūātapere for the event and final judging. Well done Thomas, and to all competitors!

And the local Tūātapere Four Square, now has the new "Sausage Capital" sausage flavour winning sausages in stock at their local store, so there are even more options to purchase "Tūātapere - Sausage Capital" sausage flavours in the township. So come and visit, and sample them all!

To quote Jo and Darren's Supreme Adventure's post on their Facebook:
"We've just spent a couple of nights in Tuatapere - the Sausage Capital of NZ. And what great timing as the national New World Best Butcher Made Sausage competition was being held in the Tui Domain on the Thursday afternoon. Needless to say Darren was extremely happy and consumed plenty of samples. His favourite the Cheeseburger Beef sausage came 1st from NW Alexandra, and mine the Smoky Beef Maple from NW Waipukurau came 2nd. A great community event with local crafts, food trucks, live music,  car display. Tuatapere is a great little town to explore, very friendly locals and some lovely little bush walks. We had drinks and dinner at the Waiau Town & Country Club, as we were fortunate to be able to stay in their backyard (NZMCA POP). Had a great yarn with a few of the locals. And of course did the essentials: groceries and laundry." (Thanks to Jo & Darren for generously sharing photos of this event for us as we couldnt attend it).


Community Contributions:
Local Dawn Egerton remembers how she helped Len deliver the LL Butchery sausages in the family milk truck while the butchers van was being repaired. She says, "Len delivered sausages to other outlets to sell them all over Southland." Dawn has also told us that she believes Len had a much bigger part to play in the famous Sausage Story than he is often given credit for. Thanks Dawn for your memories, they help illustrate this story much better.

Len was the master marketer and maker of the famous sausages, says step-son Peter Vowell, who has sent us in information saying that he believes Len was the one who made the sausage recipe. Pete, "used to work at their shop after school, boning in the butchery and grinding the stump." He also adds,
"Len was particular about perfecting the sausages as he was about most things. He was as much about animal selection on the farm, butchering (ie: resting the carcass sufficiently to old school timelines), traditional ways, choice of meat into the sausage and the important grinding and folding to the correct texture. The recipe was as much that. I recall many a conversation concerning ingredients % to introduction timing. Again, Len was sole charge. Mum did the books, Len the sausages, and both of Len & Leo, the breaking down of the animals." Interestingly, Pete continues the history and his memories with a gem of a story about Len preserving traditions, "it was Len who faced the regular scheduled visits to all butchershops concerning ingredients. At the time the Govt was controlling the food chain, in favour of Supermarket Water Injection Meat. Len held his ground, as Lead of Southland Butchers and Byproducts. He worked hard to preserve time honoured traditions." Thanks Pete for painting this picture of Len's involvement. 


More information about this Town Title will be added shortly. And more entries on these events will be going into the archive. In the meantime, please share your memories and any stories of it you know, and let us know if you have any more photos please. You can do this by adding a comment about it, at the bottom of the image page. Or contact us as per front page.


Note: these entries are compiled with information provided by donors with the records, from historical accounts and books, that gleaned from locally reported news, from national and occasionally international reports in old publications, from personal records made by the people themselves - such as their electoral enrollments, wills, war records etc., also from government and council held records like property owners, and personal information such as births, deaths and marriages or cemetery information. Lastly, from community memories, such as those passed on by friends, family and contemporaries. It is not always possible to verify memories from others, so please let us know if you believe we have any incorrect information, there is a "comment" option under this entry. at the bottom of the page. If you believe any public or personal information quoted is wrong, if you can provide proof of any alternative fact to us in a document showing evidence of the correct details, that would be very helpful to us. If we can not verify different versions of a particular story, we may publish them all. Thank you.
